meta.title: Talk more to your coding agents
meta.author: jo3_l

comments.author: edudobay
comments.text:
Nice to read something that goes in a similar direction to what I've been doing.

I also often start a discussion with the web chat (usually when it's a new idea that doesn't require analyzing existing code) and then when I'm satisfied I ask it for a summary for the next agent to implement.

I do like plan mode as a summary for the shared understanding before implementation starts. On the other hand outputting into design documents in the repository might be a better way for durable knowledge.

comments.author: peter-leonov
comments.text: Yeah, same here. Some call the context dump into a plan / progress like doc a durable compaction. It's said that compaction is bad for quality, but I argue that in harnesses compaction happens too late when LLM is close to reaching its efficient window size. While manual context dump happens, as you pointed out, when the human (or another LLM) feels like it came to a quality convergence point, thus can me folded into a well formulated set of statements.

comments.author: kprotty
comments.text:
some call it a commit message in version control /s

Recently been doing something hackily similar with a log of important context being maintained as set of md files, only to realize there's already a wheel there to use.

The md approach has advantage in segmenting the different contexes: one md for benchmarks over time, one md for changelog, another for the plan. Wonder if there's something like that in version control

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
In good designs of version control sure there is. Monotone separately stores the snapshot content of a commit, and then you attach claims — sure, there are predefined claim types like commit message / date / author (so multiple commits implementing textually the same fix will become one commit with multiple commit messages), but also you can add different stuff if you want, like I dunno, CI could later add a claim with a different claim type about the outcome of a long-running full test suite, or a later audit could add a different claim with a different type about the post-factum-discovered relevance of this commit, and so one.

Maybe a very poor version of it can be implementable with git notes. You can also implement a version of it in git with fake child commits and confuse all the naive tooling (which might be a good thing, depending on what you want to achieve?)

comments.author: peter-leonov
comments.text:
Yep, it was there right under our noses. But it's limited to the atomic progress. Anything that spans multiple commits can't live solely in commit messages.

I'd rather call our approach a "readme driven development". The main plan and key guiding principles get written down first before any code does. Plus the progress

comments.text:
Anything that spans multiple commits can't live solely in commit messages.


Branch + merge commit message for the branch?

comments.author: peter-leonov
comments.text:
After the job is done, yes indeed. But where to store the intermediate state? Right, in the filesystem, or in some metadata storage. Let alone the multi-repo story.

Anyways, Git is extensible, there must be something out there already that makes better semantic sense.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
There are better reasons to store something in a comment or documentation: commit message describes a change, comment describes the code state, they have different models of relevance.

Commit message that mentions that it unblocks this and the future steps actually could make perfect sense!

Separately, git of course has a few glaring problems when you actually want to look through the history (starting with, if reflog is useful to have, how come syncing it is not a natural thing to do).

comments.author: vinnymac
comments.text:
Surprised that Claude (and co) don’t have something like this built in.

It really is highly dependent on the task though. Not everything needs a plan, and not everything needs back and forth. Knowing what you need is in and of itself an ability many of us have built up over the years, as skilled craftsmen. It is one of those things that separates you from the pack. Most folks aren’t going to be able to know they even need to be “grilled”.
